from functools import partial

from jax import lax

import numpy as np
from scipy import ndimage

def axis_slice(ndim, index, axis):
  slices = [slice(None)] * ndim
  slices[axis] = index
  return tuple(slices)

def slice_along_axis(array, index, axis):
  return array[axis_slice(array.ndim, index, axis)]

def shift(array, offset, axis):
  index = slice(offset, None) if offset >= 0 else slice(None, offset)
  sliced = slice_along_axis(array, index, axis)
  padding = [(0, 0)] * array.ndim
  padding[axis] = (-min(offset, 0), max(offset, 0))
  return jnp.pad(sliced, padding, mode='constant', constant_values=0)

def laplacian(array, step=1):
  left = shift(array, +1, axis=0)
  right = shift(array, -1, axis=0)
  up = shift(array, +1, axis=1)
  down = shift(array, -1, axis=1)
  convolved = (left + right + up + down - 4 * array)
  if step != 1:
    convolved *= (1 / step ** 2)
  return convolved

def scalar_wave_equation(u, c=1, dx=1):
  return c ** 2 * laplacian(u, dx)

@jax.remat
def leapfrog_step(state, dt=0.5, c=1):
  # https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leapfrog_integration
  u, u_t = state
  u_tt = scalar_wave_equation(u, c)
  u_t = u_t + u_tt * dt
  u = u + u_t * dt
  return (u, u_t)

Right now, the PRNG key usage is a huge foot gun. Almost every single new use (including myself!) will incorrectly reuse the PRNG key in this way:
key = jax.random.PRNGKey(0)
a = jax.random.uniform(key, (10, 10))
b = jax.random.uniform(key, (10, 10))
Causing a and b to be the exact same values, which is very unlikely to be what a new user wants.
I am proposing a new PRNGKeyGenerator class to alleviate some of these issues. The class will basically just look like this.
class PRNGKeyGenerator():
  def __init__(self, seed):
    self._key = jax.random.PRNGKey(seed)

  def next(self):
     self._key, new_key = jax.random.split(self._key)
     return new_key
Now, (assuming all of the docs are updated), a new user would just do this instead:
keygen = jax.random.PRNGKeyGenerator(0)
a = jax.random.uniform(keygen.next(), (10, 10))
b = jax.random.uniform(keygen.next(), (10, 10))
and a and b will now have different random values. It now is less of a foot gun while still maintaining the reproducibility that JAX's random library original sought. If a user passes just keygen instead of keygen.next(), a type check can quickly detected it and crash with a very clear error.

Suppose you have an input and a source vector of size M, and a vector of input indices and output indices of N, where N>>M. The idea is that the value of the input at index input_indices[i] is to be added to the value of output at output_indices[i]. In this case, the first operation is a gather op, while the latter is a scatter-add, but an intermediate vector is required which has a memory cost of O(N) (the gather op outputs a vector of size N). and would look like this in code:
gather_output = input[input_indices]
scatter_add_output = ops.index_add(output, output_indices, gather_output)

Not sure if there's an appropriate XLA op, but if there is it'd make it considerably easier to work with large graphs when training graph neural networks, as instead of making many, many copies of node features as the output of the gather op, the results can be directly fused to the output.

As noted by https://twitter.com/peter_melchior/status/1206645602546790400 this is a notable gap in jax.numpy. We support the core fftn/ifftn routines, but basic routines like fft are the more obvious entry point, so we should make those work too.
Standard FFTs

 fft
 ifft
 fft2
 ifft2
 fftn
 ifftn

Real FFTs (see #1839)

 rfft
 irfft
 rfft2
 irfft2
 rfftn
 irfftn

Hermitian FFTs (these seem less useful, but they are easy to implement)

 hfft
 ihfft

Helper routines

 fftfreq
 rfftfreq
 fftshift (#1850)
 ifftshift (#1850)

These would be good opportunities for new contributor(s):

Easy: write fft/ifft/fft2/ifft2 in terms of fftn/ifftn.
Easy: write real-valued FFTs in terms of the complex valued FFTs.
Easy: write fftfreq/rfftfreq with jax.numpy functions.
Harder: write real-valued FFTs and their derivatives in terms of the XLA's RFFT/IRFFT.
No idea: Hermitian FFTs. I don't think the underlying primitives for these exist in XLA, and I'm not sure how widely used these actually are (I've never needed them).

Currently, matrix multiplication on TPUs (with float32 dtypes) defaults to bfloat16 multiplication with float32 accumulation. This allows for really fantastic performance for neural nets.
Using higher precision requires explicitly setting it, e.g., jax.numpy.matmul(x, y, precision=jax.lax.Precision.HIGHEST). (We could conceivably shorten this by supporting strings, e.g., jax.numpy.matmul(x, y, precision='highest'))

nodes.bodyText:
I know of two natural ways to talk about complex derivatives:


The Wirtinger derivative
For a complex number z = x + iy and a function f(z) we have two derivatives
∂f/∂z = (∂f/∂x - i ∂f/∂y)/2  and ∂f/∂z* = (∂f/∂x + i ∂f/∂y)/2


The "gradient"
∇_z(f) = ∂f/∂x + i ∂f/∂y = 2 ∂f/∂z*
which is useful in gradient descend algorithms, since it gives consists of the components of the gradient, when interpreting f as a function of two real variables f(x, y) and thus gives the direction of the steepest descend when f is a real function.


I noticed that jax.grad follows neither of these and instead computes ∂f/∂x - i ∂f/∂y = 2∂f/∂z
This is readily checked since grad(np.abs)(1j) == -1j
I feel like this is counter-intuitive and want to start a discussion, if this is indeed the behaviour that Jax should have.
I also suggest incorporating this in the Gotcha's page
nodes.title: Convention for the complex derivative
